summary: The machine has the Python runtime, DocumentDB MCP server, and a comprehensive set of DocumentDB skills (driver, indexing, vector search, local gateway guidance, Beanie quickstarts). An agent can start the sample build now. Remaining gaps are factual confusions the cold answers revealed (resource type/CLI group vs older Cosmos DB names), a missing local tool (mongosh) that helps manual verification, and several unanswered product choices (LLM provider, exact package pinning, app surface) that the builder must decide. None are blockers to coding; they require small corrective instructions or a choice during the build.
summary_points: Ready to start: python (3.13), pip, documentdb MCP server (data-plane), azure MCP server and Learn docs search are available, plus many DocumentDB skills (driver, beanie, indexing, vector-search, local-deploy).

Key confusions in cold answers: the current resource type is Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters and the CLI group is az documentdb (mongocluster) — older Cosmos DB names were conflated with this service.

Vector and full-text search answers in the cold set used non-DocumentDB syntax; the correct APIs are createIndexes with cosmosSearchOptions for vectors and createSearchIndexes + $search for BM25 full-text.
Missing useful local tooling: mongosh is not on PATH; it isn’t blocking but is recommended for manual checks.
Information gaps remain (LLM provider/model, exact package versions, sample-data provenance, whether API or CLI surface) — the builder must pick defaults and document them.

tools.workaround: Use az CLI commands and portal to inspect resources, or use pymongo/motor to query the cluster directly; but automated sample-verification scripts prefer the MCP tool.

confusions.question: What is the Azure resource provider namespace and resource type of an Azure DocumentDB cluster?
confusions.cold_answer: Resource provider namespace: Microsoft.DocumentDB. Primary resource type: Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts (resource type name: 'databaseAccounts').
confusions.grounded_answer: Current resource type for the managed MongoDB-compatible cluster is Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters (resource type 'mongoClusters').

grounding_links.title: Microsoft.DocumentDB mongoClusters (Bicep/Terraform templates)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Older Cosmos DB docs and the historical use of Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts for Cosmos accounts; both namespaces mention 'DocumentDB' and 'Cosmos', causing the model to recall the older databaseAccounts resource instead of the newer mongoClusters resource type.

confusion_sources.title: ARM/Bicep templates for mongoClusters (specific API versions)

confusions.build_risk: If the builder used databaseAccounts in templates or az CLI commands, deployment snippets would target the wrong resource type and ARM/Bicep/Terraform samples would fail or create incorrect resource types.
improvements: Update quickstarts and agent-kit samples to use Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters for cluster provisioning examples (Bicep/ARM/Terraform).
Add a deprecation note on older pages that still show Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts when the intent is to create a vCore mongo cluster.

confusions.question: Which Azure CLI command group creates and manages a cluster? Is it in the core CLI or an extension?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the built-in az cosmosdb command group (core CLI). Example: az cosmosdb create --name myAccount --resource-group rg --kind MongoDB --locations regionName=westus2. (No separate extension required.)
confusions.grounded_answer: The current CLI command group for vCore Mongo clusters is az documentdb mongocluster (e.g., az documentdb mongocluster create); az documentdb provides the mongocluster subcommands. Some cosmosdb command variants exist for compatibility, but az documentdb is the correct group for mongoClusters.

grounding_links.title: Quickstart: Create an Azure DocumentDB cluster by using Azure CLI
az documentdb mongocluster create (CLI reference)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The az cosmosdb command group historically manages Cosmos DB accounts (databaseAccounts) and older Cosmos/Mongo API examples use it; the newer first-party DocumentDB commands moved under az documentdb and expose mongocluster subcommands.

confusion_sources.title: az cosmosdb mongocluster create (older CLI group variant)

confusions.build_risk: Using az cosmosdb create would create the wrong resource type (or fail) and the build scripts that call az to inspect or patch clusters would not behave as expected.
improvements: In agent-kit CLI examples and any README quick commands, prefer az documentdb mongocluster create for vCore clusters and add a short note contrasting older az cosmosdb examples that target databaseAccounts.

confusions.question: Which Bicep and Terraform resource types deploy a cluster?
confusions.cold_answer: Bicep: resource of type Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts. Terraform (azurerm provider): azurerm_cosmosdb_account (set kind and capabilities for MongoDB).
confusions.grounded_answer: Use the Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters resource type in ARM/Bicep (or the AzAPI/AzureRM provider’s equivalent). Terraform/AVM modules and AzAPI examples target Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters (there are AVM modules for Cosmos DB for MongoDB (vCore)).

grounding_links.title: Microsoft.DocumentDB mongoClusters (Bicep/Terraform templates)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Historical overlap: many Cosmos DB provisioning docs use Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts (databaseAccounts) and azurerm_cosmosdb_account for earlier Cosmos/Cosmos Mongo API examples. The newer vCore offering uses the separate mongoClusters resource type.

confusion_sources.title: AVM / Terraform examples for Cosmos DB for MongoDB (vCore)

confusions.build_risk: IaC templates using databaseAccounts/azurerm_cosmosdb_account would not correctly create a vCore mongo cluster; the builder would provision the wrong resource shape or fail during deployment.
improvements: Add a short 'Use mongoClusters for vCore' note on the Terraform/Bicep quickstarts and in the agent kit's deployment skill; include an example Bicep snippet that uses Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters.

confusions.question: What does a connection string look like: scheme, host suffix, port, and the options it must carry?
confusions.cold_answer: Typical MongoDB-style connection string for the service: mongodb://<username>:<password>@<accountname>.mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255/?ssl=true&replicaSet=globaldb&retryWrites=false&authSource=admin. SSL/TLS is required; include replicaSet=globaldb and retryWrites=false. (Read actual URI from DOCUMENTDB_URI at runtime.)
confusions.grounded_answer: Connection strings vary by cluster type: vCore DocumentDB clusters commonly expose mongodb+srv or mongodb URIs with hostnames like <cluster>.global.mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com (or the cluster-specific host). The recommended approach: retrieve connection strings from the cluster (portal or az documentdb mongocluster list-connection-strings) and treat them as secrets; for Microsoft Entra ID use MONGODB-OIDC connection properties. Do not assume the older cosmos.mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255 pattern.

grounding_links.title: Get cluster connection strings / Connect to Azure DocumentDB using mongosh
List connection strings (az documentdb mongocluster list-connection-strings)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer describes older Cosmos DB / MongoDB API connection strings (host suffix and port patterns used there). DocumentDB vCore clusters use different host naming (mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com) and SRV-style URIs are commonly provided; Entra/OIDC also uses special authMechanism parameters.

confusion_sources.title: PowerShell example showing mongodb+srv host suffix

confusions.build_risk: Using an incorrect URI format or hard-coded port would cause connection failures; assuming replicaSet=globaldb or other parameters could be wrong for the vCore cluster and break the client’s connection code or auth path.
improvements: In quickstarts and sample README files, show the exact az documentdb mongocluster list-connection-strings command and an example of a mongodb+srv or MONGODB-OIDC connection string; advise to read DOCUMENTDB_URI from env and never store it in source.

confusions.question: How is capacity provisioned and billed: request units, compute tiers with vCores, serverless, or something else?
confusions.cold_answer: There are two common billing models: the classic Cosmos RU/s model (provisioned RUs or autoscale RUs and serverless for small usage) and a dedicated MongoDB-compatible cluster option billed by vCores/compute tier (e.g., cluster sizes like M10..M30). Use RU/s for the multi-API Cosmos accounts and vCore/compute tiers for dedicated MongoDB clusters.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct summary: Azure supports RU/s (Cosmos API, API for NoSQL) and a separate dedicated vCore/compute-tier model for Azure DocumentDB (MongoDB-compatible vCore clusters). DocumentDB vCore clusters are billed by compute tier (M-series vCores) + storage; RU/s is not the billing model for vCore clusters.

grounding_links.title: Azure DocumentDB pricing explained (compute and storage / vCore tiers)
Convert vCores to RU/s (guidance showing difference between RU and vCore models)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The model mixed the distinct billing models for Cosmos RU-based accounts and the vCore (DocumentDB) offering; both are in the broader Cosmos/DocumentDB family and have overlapping documentation, which invites confusion.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder assumed RU/s for provisioning a vCore sample, cost/size guidance and sample configuration would be wrong (wrong defaults, misleading README statements about how to size the cluster).
improvements: Document the billing model in the sample README: 'This sample targets an existing vCore DocumentDB cluster billed by compute tier (M-series) + storage — do not attempt to specify RU/s for provisioning.'

confusions.question: Which authentication methods are supported, and how does a driver authenticate with Microsoft Entra ID?
confusions.cold_answer: Primary data-plane auth is via MongoDB credentials (username/password / SCRAM) created on the account; drivers connect with standard MongoDB auth in the connection string. Management and RBAC use Microsoft Entra ID (Azure AD). If Entra ID data-plane auth is supported, drivers obtain an Azure AD access token and present it via the driver SASL/OAUTHBEARER or an auth mechanism the service advertises; however in practice for MongoDB API you normally use the Mongo user credentials (SCRAM) and Azure AD is used for control-plane/management and role assignment. (If you need Entra ID data-plane auth, request a token and pass according to the Mongo driver’s SASL/OAUTHBEARER flow.)
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB supports native (SCRAM) authentication and Microsoft Entra ID (OIDC) for data-plane access. Entra ID (MicrosoftEntraID) is enabled per-cluster (authConfig.allowedModes) and clients use OIDC (authMechanism=MONGODB-OIDC) or a driver callback (OIDC token callback) to present an Entra-issued token; the docs include exact connection-string examples for MongoDB Compass / mongosh and Python (using Azure Identity and OIDC callbacks).

grounding_links.title: Connect to Azure DocumentDB using role-based access control and Microsoft Entra ID (how-to, OIDC examples)
Enable Microsoft Entra ID authentication on a cluster (az resource patch example)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer treated Azure AD as only control-plane; in reality DocumentDB supports Entra data-plane auth via OIDC with explicit connection-string/authMechanism properties. The older Cosmos/Mongo API docs and native SCRAM usage examples add to the ambiguity.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder assumes only SCRAM is available, they may hard-code DB users or avoid recommending managed identity flows; conversely, using Entra/OIDC without enabling it on the cluster will cause auth failures.
improvements: Add a short sample showing both approaches in the quickstart: (1) native SCRAM example and (2) OIDC example using azure-identity DefaultAzureCredential and the driver OIDC callback, with links to the docs above.

confusions.question: Which client library should an application use? Is there a service-specific SDK?
confusions.cold_answer: Use standard MongoDB drivers/libraries for your language (e.g., pymongo/motor for Python). For ODM in Python use Beanie (on top of Motor) or MongoEngine. There is an Azure management SDK for Cosmos DB control-plane, but for data-plane MongoDB API use the MongoDB-compatible drivers (no special service-specific data-plane SDK required).
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct: Use standard MongoDB drivers for data-plane access (pymongo/motor for Python). For Beanie, the quickstart recommends a PyMongo Async client or Beanie 2 tested with PyMongo Async; management/control-plane tasks use Azure Resource Manager SDKs or az CLI.

grounding_links.title: Quickstart: Connect Beanie to Azure DocumentDB
Quickstart: Use Azure DocumentDB with MongoDB driver for Python

confusions.question: Which vector index types are supported, and what does the command that creates one look like?
confusions.cold_answer: On the vector-capable cluster the supported index algorithms include HNSW, IVF and DiskANN. The Mongo-style command to create a vector index is like: db.mycoll.createIndex({ embedding: 'vector' }, { vector: { dims: 1536, algorithm: 'hnsw', metric: 'cosine' } }). (Use your actual dims and algorithm name in the index options.)
confusions.grounded_answer: DocumentDB supports vector-ivf, vector-hnsw, and vector-diskann index kinds. The createIndexes command is used with a cosmosSearch / cosmosSearchOptions shape; example: db.runCommand({ createIndexes: 'mycoll', indexes: [{ name: 'v1', key: { 'embedding': 'cosmosSearch' }, cosmosSearchOptions: { kind: 'vector-hnsw', dimensions: 1536, similarity: 'COS' } }] });

grounding_links.title: Integrated vector store in Azure DocumentDB (createIndexes / cosmosSearchOptions examples)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer used a MongoDB server-style createIndex signature with a 'vector' key type that an open-source MongoDB extension might use; DocumentDB uses a createIndexes command with cosmosSearchOptions to create vector indexes.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder used the wrong createIndex syntax, index creation would fail and vector search queries would not work; the sample's seed script could error out during index creation.
improvements: Replace any createIndex vector examples in agent-kit docs with the createIndexes + cosmosSearchOptions template shown in the Vector Search docs.

confusions.question: How are full-text search and hybrid search done?
confusions.cold_answer: For basic text search use MongoDB text indexes (db.collection.createIndex({field: 'text'})). For large/full-featured search and hybrid vector+text scenarios, integrate with Azure Cognitive Search (index the data via change feed or an indexer) or use the service's built-in vector indexes combined with field filters in aggregation; hybrid vector+semantic search is done by combining a vector index lookup with traditional text filters in the application/aggregation pipeline.
confusions.grounded_answer: DocumentDB provides its own full-text search (BM25) via search indexes created with createSearchIndexes and queried with $search (BM25) as the first stage of an aggregation pipeline; hybrid search is done by combining BM25 search indexes with vector searches (cosmosSearch) and fusing results (Reciprocal Rank Fusion or server-side $unionWith construction). While MongoDB text indexes are supported for simpler cases, the recommended preview full-text search uses createSearchIndexes + $search for BM25, custom analyzers and hybrid RRF patterns.

grounding_links.title: Full-text search in Azure DocumentDB (createSearchIndexes + $search and hybrid search guidance)
Hybrid search (BM25 + vector fusion)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer defaulted to the familiar MongoDB text index approach and suggested Cognitive Search as an external option; DocumentDB's newer full-text engine (createSearchIndexes and $search) is a first-class, integrated option for BM25 and hybrid retrieval.

confusion_sources.title: Text indexes vs full-text search guidance

confusions.build_risk: If the builder uses only MongoDB text indexes, they miss the BM25-ranked preview search features and hybrid RRF patterns that the sample should demonstrate; results and sample code would not match the intended behavior.
improvements: In sample README and agent-kit guidance, recommend createSearchIndexes + $search for full-text BM25 and show a small example for hybrid BM25+vector fusion (RRF).

confusions.question: Which MongoDB wire protocol or server versions are supported, and which commonly used MongoDB features are not?
confusions.cold_answer: Supported wire/server versions depend on the account type; managed MongoDB-compatible clusters commonly support modern MongoDB wire versions (examples: 4.x, 5.x, 6.x and on dedicated clusters 7.0). However not every MongoDB server feature is supported: some admin commands, server-side JavaScript, and certain extension features (Atlas Search, server-side file storage) are not available or are implemented differently. Transactions are supported in many configurations but may have limitations in sharded/dedicated setups. Expect to use standard MongoDB drivers but verify feature availability for advanced server-side features.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB supports MongoDB wire protocol/server versions 5.0, 6.0, 7.0 and 8.0 (documented compatibility); most MongoDB drivers and common aggregation operators are supported, but a small set of admin or server-level commands and some driver-specific features differ — the compatibility docs list unsupported operators and commands. Change streams are supported on compatible server versions.

grounding_links.title: Compare Azure DocumentDB to MongoDB Atlas (wire protocol versions and compatibility)
MongoDB Query Language (MQL) compatibility in Azure DocumentDB (operators list)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer was vague; it did not state the officially supported wire protocol versions. The model hedged rather than returning the documented range 5.0–8.0.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder assumes a different server version, they might pick incompatible driver features or resort to wrong syntax (e.g., using very new operator features that aren't supported in the chosen server compatibility mode).
improvements: Add an explicit compatibility note in the agent kit and sample README: 'This sample assumes a DocumentDB cluster with MongoDB wire protocol 7.0 (or list supported versions) — verify with the cluster admin or az documentdb mongocluster show.'

confusions.question: How do you run the database locally for development and tests: which image or emulator, and which port?
confusions.cold_answer: There is no full-featured local emulator that perfectly emulates the service's MongoDB API and vector features. For local development run a standard MongoDB Docker image (e.g., mongo:7.0) on port 27017. For Cosmos DB-specific behavior you must test against the real cluster; the Azure Cosmos DB emulator does not fully support the MongoDB API/vector features in parity with the managed service.
confusions.grounded_answer: There is an official DocumentDB Gateway Docker image for local development (ghcr.io/documentdb/documentdb/documentdb-local:latest), which exposes the MongoDB wire protocol on port 10260 and PostgreSQL on 9712; the documentdb-local-deployment guidance recommends using that Gateway image for app development to get better parity than a vanilla mongo:7 container.

grounding_links.title: documentdb-local-deployment

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer reflected the general assumption that an official emulator does not exist and recommended a generic mongo image; in fact the DocumentDB project provides a Gateway Docker image that is the recommended local runtime and exposes Mongo on port 10260.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder used mongo:7.0 on 27017 for local dev, vector/search behavior and TLS/auth details may differ from the DocumentDB Gateway, causing parity issues in local tests.
improvements: Add 'use the DocumentDB gateway image on port 10260 for local dev' to the sample README and seed scripts, and refer to the documentdb-local-deployment skill for compose examples.

confusions.question: Are change streams supported, and does anything have to be enabled first?
confusions.cold_answer: Change streams are supported on MongoDB-compatible accounts/cluster types that implement the necessary replication/OPLOG semantics (typically dedicated clusters or newer wire-version accounts). If not supported, use the Cosmos DB change feed (Core API) as an alternative. In some account types you may need to enable a capability or use a dedicated cluster SKU for change streams to be available.
confusions.grounded_answer: Change streams are supported in Azure DocumentDB for compatible server versions (>= 3.6 historically and for current supported versions); the compatibility docs and change-stream guidance confirm change streams API availability. For migrations and some account types you must use a cluster/server version that supports change streams.

grounding_links.title: Change streams in Azure Cosmos DB’s API for MongoDB

confusions.question: Which MCP server gives an agent data-plane tools for this service? Does the general Azure MCP Server cover it?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the 'documentdb' MCP server (the documentdb MCP server) for data-plane tools and inspection of DocumentDB (Cosmos DB / Mongo API) accounts. The general azure MCP server does not replace the service-specific documentdb MCP server for specialized data-plane operations such as inspecting vector indexes and query plans for this service.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct: the 'documentdb' MCP server provides data-plane tools (list_databases, create_index, aggregate, explain, list_indexes, etc.). The general 'azure' MCP server is complementary (control-plane) but does not supply specialized data-plane actions for vector/index inspection.

grounding_links.title: documentdb

confusions.question: What was this service called before, and how does it relate to Azure Cosmos DB and to the open-source DocumentDB project?
confusions.cold_answer: Microsoft's original managed JSON document DB service was branded DocumentDB; that technology evolved into Azure Cosmos DB. The MongoDB-compatible offering is an API on top of Cosmos DB (historically called 'Azure Cosmos DB for MongoDB' or 'Cosmos DB's MongoDB API'). The open-source 'DocumentDB' (if referenced elsewhere) is different; the Microsoft DocumentDB name was a predecessor to Cosmos DB rather than the open-source project.
confusions.grounded_answer: Partly correct but incomplete: Azure DocumentDB (with MongoDB compatibility) is the current first-party managed Mongo-compatible service; historically the Cosmos DB brand and 'Cosmos DB for MongoDB' were used, and earlier marketing used 'DocumentDB'. Additionally, DocumentDB is now an open-source engine (DocumentDB OSS) that underlies the service and is distinct from Amazon DocumentDB (AWS). Clarify: 'Azure DocumentDB' is Microsoft’s vCore-managed MongoDB-compatible offering and is built on the open-source DocumentDB engine (not the same as Amazon DocumentDB).

grounding_links.title: What is Azure DocumentDB (overview & OSS engine)
DocumentDB: The Open-Source Engine Powering Azure DocumentDB

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The name 'DocumentDB' has historically been used by Microsoft (and in the Cosmos lineage) and separately there's an open-source DocumentDB project; older documentation and brand renames (DocumentDB → Cosmos DB) and multiple overlapping names cause the model to conflate the histories.
confusions.build_risk: A builder referencing older 'Cosmos DB' or 'databaseAccounts' documentation may pick the wrong ARM resource type or CLI commands and publish samples that fail to apply to the vCore offering.
improvements: Add a short 'naming & lineage' paragraph to quickstarts and README files clarifying: 'Azure DocumentDB (vCore, MongoDB-compatible) is a first-party Azure service built on the open-source DocumentDB engine; it is distinct from Amazon DocumentDB and from older Cosmos DB databaseAccounts samples.'

confusions.question: What engine is underneath, and does that change anything in application code?
confusions.cold_answer: Underneath is Microsoft’s Cosmos DB engine exposing a MongoDB wire-protocol compatibility layer for the MongoDB API. That means application code uses standard MongoDB drivers and typical MongoDB idioms, but some server-level behaviors and advanced features may differ (limits, unsupported admin commands, and different consistency/transaction semantics). Test against the managed cluster for any advanced features.
confusions.grounded_answer: Incorrect: Azure DocumentDB (the managed Mongo-compatible service) is built on the open-source DocumentDB engine (DocumentDB OSS) which is built on PostgreSQL internals; it provides a MongoDB wire-protocol compatibility layer. Applications should use standard MongoDB drivers, but the underlying engine is DocumentDB OSS, not the Cosmos DB Core engine — this affects some admin and operational behaviors and licensing considerations.

grounding_links.title: DocumentDB: The Open-Source Engine Powering Azure DocumentDB (OSS)
What is Azure DocumentDB (overview)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The model conflated Azure DocumentDB with the Cosmos DB engine historically used for the multi-API Cosmos product; the updated DocumentDB product uses the DocumentDB OSS engine (PostgreSQL-based) which is distinct from Cosmos DB's NoSQL engine.

confusion_sources.title: Compare Azure DocumentDB to MongoDB Atlas (engine & compatibility notes)

confusions.build_risk: If the builder assumes Cosmos DB core internals, they may recommend wrong operational procedures, or misunderstand index/feature parity; sample code (drivers, connection strings) remains MongoDB-compatible, but operational guidance and migration notes must target DocumentDB OSS.
improvements: Add an explicit 'engine' note in the agent kit and every quickstart: 'Azure DocumentDB runs the open-source DocumentDB engine (built on PostgreSQL) and exposes a MongoDB wire-protocol interface; use MongoDB drivers but consult DocumentDB OSS docs for engine-specific behaviors.'

confusions.question: What index definition does this sample need for vector search (embedding field) to support nearest-neighbour queries?
confusions.cold_answer: Create a vector index on the embedding field: db.reports.createIndex({ embedding: 'vector' }, { vector: { dims: 1536, algorithm: 'hnsw', metric: 'cosine' } }). (Adjust dims to your embedding size; algorithm 'hnsw' used in this sample.)
confusions.grounded_answer: Use db.runCommand({ createIndexes: 'reports', indexes: [{ name: 'embedding_vec', key: { 'embedding': 'cosmosSearch' }, cosmosSearchOptions: { kind: 'vector-hnsw', dimensions: <dims>, similarity: 'COS' } }] }); (Or kind 'vector-ivf' / 'vector-diskann' with the corresponding options.)

grounding_links.title: Vector index creation examples (HNSW/IVF/DiskANN)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer used a MongoDB server-style vector index API that doesn't match DocumentDB's createIndexes + cosmosSearchOptions syntax.
confusions.build_risk: Wrong index creation leads to API errors at runtime and prevents vector queries from running in the sample.
improvements: Replace vector index examples in sample templates with the createIndexes + cosmosSearchOptions template and provide a small helper function in the repo to create a vector index using the correct command.

confusions.question: What aggregation pipeline will surface the most frequently reported events by drug?
confusions.cold_answer: [ { $match: {} }, { $group: { _id: { drug: '$drug', event: '$event' }, count: { $sum: 1 } } }, { $group: { _id: '$_id.drug', events: { $push: { event: '$_id.event', count: '$count' } } } }, { $project: { drug: '$_id', topEvents: { $slice: [ { $sortArray: { input: '$events', sortBy: { count: -1 } } }, 10 ] } } } ]
confusions.grounded_answer: This pipeline is valid in DocumentDB: group by (drug,event) to count occurrences, then group by drug to assemble event lists, use $sortArray to sort events by count and $slice to keep top N. An alternative is to use $group then $sort and $limit on a per-drug aggregation via $group + $push + $sortArray or via $facet per drug; the suggested pipeline is supported (operators like $sortArray are supported).

confusions.question: What Beanie/Pydantic document schema will this sample use to store validated adverse-event documents?
confusions.cold_answer: Pydantic/Beanie model: class AdverseEvent(Document): drug: str; event: str; severity: str; onset_date: datetime.date; text: str; embedding: Optional[List[float]] = None; class Settings: name = 'reports' and use database 'sample_healthcare_18'.
confusions.grounded_answer: This Beanie/Pydantic model is appropriate: a Document model with drug, event, severity, onset_date (ISO date/datetime), original text, optional embedding, and Settings.name referencing the 'reports' (or 'adverse_events') collection in database 'sample_healthcare_18'.

confusions.question: How should the sample read the cluster connection string at runtime?
confusions.cold_answer: Read the MongoDB URI from the environment variable DOCUMENTDB_URI (e.g., uri = os.environ['DOCUMENTDB_URI']) and pass it unchanged to motor.AsyncIOMotorClient or pymongo.MongoClient. Do not hard-code credentials or write the URI to disk; provide a .env.example with a placeholder.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct: read the connection URI from an environment variable (the run environment uses DOCUMENTDB_URI), use it to initialize the driver client (pymongo AsyncMongoClient or motor), and avoid writing secrets to source control; include a .env.example with placeholders.

confusions.question: What exact command will I use locally to inspect collections and indexes with the documentdb MCP server?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the documentdb MCP server CLI: mcp server documentdb --profile default inspect-collection --database sample_healthcare_18 --collection reports (or the equivalent mcp documentdb inspect-collection --profile default --db sample_healthcare_18 --coll reports).
confusions.grounded_answer: The documentdb MCP server provides commands to inspect collections and indexes; the machine inventory documents the documentdb MCP server with tools like documentdb_list_indexes and documentdb_get_statistics. Use the documentdb MCP server's inspect/list-indexes style command (or use the documentdb MCP server helpers in the agent toolkit) with the 'default' profile as documented in the agent kit.

information_gaps.title: LLM provider and model selection
information_gaps.description: The sample prompt asks to use prompt engineering and an LLM to extract fields, but no provider or model is specified (OpenAI/Azure OpenAI, Anthropic, Claude, local LLM). I searched the skills and docs for guidance and found no definitive recommended provider for this sample; the builder must choose and document the provider, model name, authentication, and any rate/latency expectations.

information_gaps.title: Exact Python package versions to pin
information_gaps.description: The prompt and installed skills recommend Beanie and pymongo/PyMongo Async or Motor, but do not prescribe exact package versions to pin in requirements.txt. I reviewed the Beanie quickstart but the sample runtime (Python 3.13) needs pinned, tested versions for beanie/pymongo/motor and any LLM client to guarantee reproducible builds.

information_gaps.title: App surface (API vs CLI) decision
information_gaps.description: The prompt doesn't state whether to expose a FastAPI HTTP endpoint or a CLI to accept free-text reports; the prompt review assumed a FastAPI API but neither the skills nor docs decide this for the builder. The builder must choose the surface and document it in the README.

information_gaps.title: Sample data provenance and licensing
information_gaps.description: No authoritative sample dataset or license is provided for adverse-event text samples. The builder must either generate synthetic examples (documented as synthetic/CC0) or obtain a properly licensed dataset; I searched skills/docs and found no sample data source.

information_gaps.title: Integration test strategy for live cluster
information_gaps.description: Run environment forbids provisioning a new cluster and indicates tests should run against the live cluster; but no test strategy (mocking vs integration tests) is provided. The builder needs a guidance page saying which tests run offline vs which require DOCUMENTDB_URI and how to mark/guard integration tests.

guidance_for_builder.instruction: Use the resource type Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters for vCore MongoDB clusters in ARM/Bicep/Terraform and the az documentdb mongocluster CLI group when creating or managing clusters; do not use databaseAccounts or az cosmosdb for provisioning vCore clusters.

guidance_for_builder.instruction: Read the connection string from DOCUMENTDB_URI at runtime and treat it as a secret; when creating vector indexes use db.runCommand({ createIndexes: 'collection', indexes: [ { key: { embedding: 'cosmosSearch' }, cosmosSearchOptions: { kind: 'vector-hnsw'|'vector-ivf'|'vector-diskann', dimensions: <dims>, similarity: 'COS'|'L2'|'IP' } } ] }); and for full-text/BM25 use createSearchIndexes + $search.

guidance_for_builder.instruction: If you want passwordless or managed-identity access, enable Microsoft Entra ID (authConfig.allowedModes includes MicrosoftEntraID) and use the OIDC connection pattern (authMechanism=MONGODB-OIDC with the driver OIDC callback or MONGODB-OIDC properties) — otherwise use native SCRAM credentials. Test both paths in README and CI instructions.

guidance_for_builder.instruction: For local development, use the DocumentDB Gateway Docker image (recommended) which exposes Mongo on port 10260 (see documentdb-local-deployment skill), not a plain mongo:7.0 container, to get better parity for vector/search and auth behavior.

inventory_recommendations.name: azd
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Not required for this sample because the run environment provides a live cluster and the sample will not provision resources. If IaC/deployment workflows are later added, install azd via the platform package manager or from https://aka.ms/azd/install.

inventory_recommendations.name: bicep
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Not required for this sample because the cluster is provided and no in-run provisioning is needed. If builders want to include Bicep IaC examples, add bicep CLI to PATH or use az cli's built-in bicep features (az bicep build).

inventory_recommendations.name: terraform
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Not needed for this sample run; if the team later includes Terraform examples for provisioning mongoClusters, install Terraform on PATH and consider using AzAPI/AzureRM providers and the AVM module referenced in docs.

inventory_recommendations.name: dotnet
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Not required for this Python sample. Add dotnet if you plan to provide .NET sample variants.

inventory_recommendations.name: mongosh
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Install mongosh on PATH. It is useful for manual connectivity checks, creating sample indexes, and ad-hoc verification during development; install from MongoDB downloads or your platform package manager and use the cluster's connection string from the portal or az documentdb mongocluster list-connection-strings to connect.
